subtopic_detail: Chronic hepatitis C assessment before direct acting antiviral therapy
stem:
A 38 year old man attends your general practice after a positive hepatitis C antibody test arranged at a needle and syringe program. He injected heroin between the ages of 19 and 27 and has not injected for 11 years. He drinks four standard drinks each week and takes no regular medicines.

He feels well and works full time. Abdominal examination is unremarkable with no palpable spleen, no ascites and no stigmata of chronic liver disease. He is anxious about the cost of treatment and asks whether he needs to see a specialist before anything can start. His hepatitis B surface antigen is negative and he is immune to hepatitis A.

data_table.Investigations: Hepatitis C RNA detected, genotype not performed; alanine aminotransferase 68 U/L (less than 40); bilirubin within normal limits; albumin 41 g/L (35-50); platelets 212 x10^9/L (150-400); international normalised ratio 1.0 (0.8-1.2)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer to a hepatologist for genotyping before any antiviral therapy is considered
options.rationale: Genotyping is no longer required because current regimens are pangenotypic, and referral would delay a treatment that a general practitioner can prescribe. Specialist referral is reserved for cirrhosis, previous treatment failure or coinfection. (Source: Australian Recommendations for the Management of Hepatitis C Virus Infection)
source_refs: Australian Recommendations for the Management of Hepatitis C Virus Infection

options.text: Repeat the hepatitis C antibody test in three months to confirm true infection
options.rationale: A detectable hepatitis C RNA already confirms current infection, so repeating the antibody adds nothing and simply defers care. Repeat antibody testing is used to detect seroconversion after a recent exposure, not to confirm established viraemia. (Source: Australian Recommendations for the Management of Hepatitis C Virus Infection)
source_refs: Australian Recommendations for the Management of Hepatitis C Virus Infection

options.text: Assess for cirrhosis, then prescribe a pangenotypic direct acting antiviral course
options.rationale: Treatment is subsidised and can be initiated in primary care, and the only assessment that alters the regimen and the follow up plan is whether cirrhosis is present, judged by non-invasive scoring or transient elastography. His normal albumin, platelets and clotting make advanced fibrosis unlikely but it still needs formal assessment. (Source: Australian Recommendations for the Management of Hepatitis C Virus Infection)
source_refs: Australian Recommendations for the Management of Hepatitis C Virus Infection
Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Viral Hepatitis

options.text: Advise six months of alcohol abstinence and reassess his liver enzymes after that
options.rationale: His intake is within low risk drinking limits and abstinence is not a prerequisite for antiviral therapy, so this delays cure without benefit. Alcohol reduction advice matters for fibrosis progression but does not gate treatment. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Viral Hepatitis)
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Viral Hepatitis

options.text: Arrange liver biopsy to stage fibrosis before deciding on antiviral treatment
options.rationale: Biopsy has been replaced by non-invasive fibrosis assessment such as elastography or serum scoring, and its risks are not justified when the treatment decision does not depend on histology. Biopsy is retained only where a competing liver diagnosis is suspected. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Viral Hepatitis)
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Viral Hepatitis

explanation.summary: Australia subsidises pangenotypic direct acting antiviral therapy for all adults with chronic hepatitis C, and any medical practitioner can prescribe it, which was the central change that made elimination targets realistic. A reactive antibody indicates exposure only, so a hepatitis C RNA test is required to establish current infection and to distinguish it from spontaneous clearance. Pre-treatment work up is deliberately minimal: confirm viraemia, assess for cirrhosis using non-invasive methods, screen for hepatitis B and check for drug interactions. Cirrhosis matters because it changes regimen duration and commits the patient to six monthly hepatocellular carcinoma surveillance that continues even after cure. Sustained virological response is confirmed by an undetectable RNA 12 weeks after completing therapy.
key_points: A reactive antibody requires a hepatitis C RNA test to confirm current infection
Current regimens are pangenotypic, so genotyping is not needed before treatment
General practitioners can prescribe subsidised therapy without specialist referral in uncomplicated cases
Cirrhosis assessment uses non-invasive scoring or elastography rather than biopsy
Cure does not end surveillance in cirrhosis, where six monthly imaging continues
explanation.pearls: Screen for hepatitis B surface antigen before starting direct acting antivirals, because clearing hepatitis C can trigger hepatitis B reactivation, and confirm cure with a hepatitis C RNA taken 12 weeks after the last dose.

sources.label: Australian Recommendations for the Management of Hepatitis C Virus Infection
Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Viral Hepatitis

subtopic_detail: Risk stratification of incidental hepatic steatosis on ultrasound
stem:
A 56 year old woman is referred to you after an abdominal ultrasound performed for right sided abdominal discomfort reported a bright liver consistent with fatty infiltration and no gallstones. She has type 2 diabetes on metformin, a body mass index of 34 kg/m2 and treated hypertension.

She drinks two standard drinks per month. Hepatitis B and C serology, iron studies, antinuclear antibody and coeliac serology have all returned negative or within normal limits. She has no palpable spleen, no ascites and no spider naevi. She asks whether the fatty liver matters and what should happen next.

data_table.Investigations: Alanine aminotransferase 46 U/L (less than 40), aspartate aminotransferase 39 U/L (less than 40), platelets 168 x10^9/L (150-400), albumin 40 g/L (35-50), HbA1c 7.6 per cent (less than 6.0)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her assessment?

options.text: Repeat the liver ultrasound in 12 months to see whether the steatosis has progressed
options.rationale: Ultrasound detects fat but cannot grade fibrosis, which is the feature that determines outcome, so serial scanning tracks the wrong variable. Repeat imaging has a role in hepatocellular carcinoma surveillance once cirrhosis is established. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Non-alcoholic Fatty Liver Disease)
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Non-alcoholic Fatty Liver Disease

options.text: Calculate a FIB-4 score and arrange transient elastography if it is not low risk
options.rationale: Fibrosis stage, not the presence of fat or the transaminase level, predicts liver related and overall mortality, and the recommended pathway begins with a simple serum score using age, transaminases and platelets before proceeding to elastography. Her diabetes places her in the group where active fibrosis assessment is specifically advised. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Non-alcoholic Fatty Liver Disease)
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Non-alcoholic Fatty Liver Disease
BMJ Best Practice: Non-alcoholic Fatty Liver Disease

options.text: Reassure her that near normal transaminases exclude significant liver fibrosis
options.rationale: Transaminases correlate poorly with fibrosis stage and can be normal in established cirrhosis, so a near normal alanine aminotransferase is not a rule-out. Enzyme levels are more useful for detecting a superimposed drug or viral injury. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Non-alcoholic Fatty Liver Disease)
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Non-alcoholic Fatty Liver Disease

options.text: Cease metformin because of the risk of drug related hepatic injury in fatty liver
options.rationale: Metformin is not hepatotoxic in this setting and stopping it worsens the metabolic drivers of the liver disease itself. Drug cessation would be considered for agents with a recognised cholestatic or hepatocellular signature. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)
source_refs: Australian Medicines Handbook

options.text: Refer directly for liver biopsy to determine whether steatohepatitis is present
options.rationale: Biopsy is invasive and reserved for cases where non-invasive assessment is discordant or a competing diagnosis is suspected, so it should not be the first step. Distinguishing simple steatosis from steatohepatitis rarely changes initial management. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Non-alcoholic Fatty Liver Disease)
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Non-alcoholic Fatty Liver Disease

explanation.summary: Hepatic steatosis is common and most patients never develop liver related complications, so the clinical task is to identify the minority with advanced fibrosis rather than to treat the fat itself. Australian pathways use a two step approach in which a simple serum score calculated from age, both transaminases and the platelet count triages patients, and only those above the low risk cut-off proceed to transient elastography or specialist referral. Type 2 diabetes is the single strongest predictor of advanced fibrosis in this population, which is why these patients are actively assessed rather than reassured. Management centres on weight reduction of seven to ten per cent, optimisation of glycaemic and cardiovascular risk, and alcohol minimisation. Cardiovascular disease, not liver failure, remains the leading cause of death in this group.
key_points: Fibrosis stage predicts outcome; the amount of steatosis and the transaminase level do not
Normal transaminases do not exclude advanced fibrosis or cirrhosis
A serum fibrosis score is the recommended first triage step before elastography
Type 2 diabetes markedly raises the probability of advanced fibrosis
Cardiovascular disease is the commonest cause of death in this population
explanation.pearls: FIB-4 uses age, both aminotransferases and the platelet count: a value below 1.30 makes advanced fibrosis unlikely and needs only risk factor management, while a value above 2.67 warrants elastography and specialist referral.

sources.label: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Non-alcoholic Fatty Liver Disease
BMJ Best Practice: Non-alcoholic Fatty Liver Disease

subtopic_detail: Isolated unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia in a well young adult
stem:
A 22 year old university student is referred to you after a pre-employment medical showed a raised bilirubin. He recalls being told he looked slightly yellow during a bout of gastroenteritis two years ago, when he had eaten little for two days. He feels well, takes no medicines and has never injected drugs.

He has no abdominal pain, no dark urine and no pale stools. Examination shows mild scleral icterus, no hepatomegaly, no splenomegaly and no lymphadenopathy. A blood film is reported as normal with no spherocytes, no fragments and no polychromasia.

data_table.Investigations: Total bilirubin 58 micromol/L (less than 20) with conjugated fraction 6 micromol/L; alanine aminotransferase, aspartate aminotransferase, alkaline phosphatase and gamma-glutamyl transferase all within normal limits; haemoglobin 148 g/L (130-175), reticulocytes 62 x10^9/L (20-100), lactate dehydrogenase within normal limits, haptoglobin within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Hereditary spherocytosis with chronic compensated extravascular haemolysis
options.rationale: Haemolysis is excluded by a normal reticulocyte count with normal lactate dehydrogenase and preserved haptoglobin, and the film shows no spherocytes or splenomegaly. This diagnosis would be supported by anaemia with a raised reticulocyte count and a family history of gallstones. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Assessment of Jaundice)
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Assessment of Jaundice

options.text: Gilbert syndrome causing reduced hepatic bilirubin conjugation during fasting
options.rationale: Isolated unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia with entirely normal liver enzymes, no haemolysis and jaundice provoked by fasting or intercurrent illness is the characteristic pattern of reduced glucuronyl transferase activity. The condition is benign and needs no treatment or ongoing monitoring. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Abnormal Liver Function Tests)
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Abnormal Liver Function Tests
BMJ Best Practice: Assessment of Jaundice

options.text: Dubin-Johnson syndrome causing impaired biliary excretion of conjugated pigment
options.rationale: This defect produces a predominantly conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia, whereas his conjugated fraction is only 6 micromol/L, and the two conditions are separated precisely by which fraction is elevated. It would also typically show a pigmented liver on biopsy. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Assessment of Jaundice)
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Assessment of Jaundice

options.text: Primary sclerosing cholangitis producing early intrahepatic biliary obstruction
options.rationale: Cholestatic disease raises the alkaline phosphatase and gamma-glutamyl transferase and elevates the conjugated fraction, none of which is present. It should be considered when cholestatic enzymes rise, particularly alongside inflammatory bowel disease. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Abnormal Liver Function Tests)
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Abnormal Liver Function Tests

options.text: Chronic hepatitis B infection in the immune tolerant phase of the disease
options.rationale: Immune tolerant infection is characterised by high viral load with normal enzymes and a normal bilirubin, so it does not explain isolated jaundice. Serology would be needed to exclude it only if there were risk factors or enzyme abnormalities. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Abnormal Liver Function Tests)
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Abnormal Liver Function Tests

explanation.summary: The first branch point in any jaundiced patient is whether the hyperbilirubinaemia is predominantly unconjugated or conjugated, because that single split separates prehepatic and conjugation defects from hepatocellular and cholestatic disease. Unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia arises either from increased bilirubin production, as in haemolysis or resolving haematoma, or from reduced conjugation, and the reticulocyte count with lactate dehydrogenase and haptoglobin distinguishes them. Gilbert syndrome affects around five per cent of the population, results from reduced uridine diphosphate glucuronosyltransferase activity, and becomes clinically visible during fasting, intercurrent illness, dehydration or physical stress. It requires no treatment, but recognising it prevents an expensive and anxiety-provoking hepatology work up. It also has a practical drug interaction dimension, since the same enzyme deficiency alters the metabolism of certain chemotherapy and antiretroviral agents.
key_points: Fractionate the bilirubin first: unconjugated versus conjugated redirects the entire work up
Normal reticulocytes, lactate dehydrogenase and haptoglobin exclude significant haemolysis
Gilbert syndrome shows entirely normal liver enzymes with jaundice provoked by fasting or illness
Dubin-Johnson and Rotor syndromes cause conjugated, not unconjugated, hyperbilirubinaemia
No treatment or surveillance is needed once the diagnosis is established
explanation.pearls: Reduced glucuronosyltransferase activity in Gilbert syndrome also impairs irinotecan metabolism, raising the risk of severe neutropenia and diarrhoea, so the diagnosis should be flagged before that agent is prescribed.

sources.label: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Abnormal Liver Function Tests
BMJ Best Practice: Assessment of Jaundice

subtopic_detail: Recognising serious drug induced liver injury and the decision to cease therapy
stem:
You are the medical registrar reviewing a 63 year old woman in clinic. She completed a two week course of amoxicillin with clavulanate for a dental infection five weeks ago and now describes two weeks of nausea, itch and dark coloured urine. She takes perindopril and atorvastatin, both unchanged for four years, and no herbal or over the counter preparations.

She drinks minimal alcohol. Examination shows jaundice and scratch marks over her forearms, with a soft non-tender abdomen and no ascites or hepatomegaly. Abdominal ultrasound shows a normal liver texture and no biliary dilatation, and viral hepatitis serology and autoimmune screen are negative.

data_table.Investigations: Bilirubin 96 micromol/L (less than 20), alanine aminotransferase 412 U/L (less than 40), alkaline phosphatase 310 U/L (30-110), international normalised ratio 1.1 (0.8-1.2), albumin 38 g/L (35-50), eosinophils 0.8 x10^9/L (0.0-0.5)

lead_in: Which action is most important in her management?

options.text: Cease atorvastatin and monitor her liver biochemistry weekly until it normalises
options.rationale: Statins cause a mild transaminase rise early after initiation and are an implausible culprit after four unchanged years with this degree of jaundice. Withdrawing the statin would leave the true agent unrecognised on her record. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)
source_refs: Australian Medicines Handbook

options.text: Record a permanent allergy alert for the implicated agent and monitor her recovery
options.rationale: The mixed hepatocellular and cholestatic pattern with eosinophilia arising weeks after amoxicillin with clavulanate is the classic latency and signature of that agent, and because rechallenge can cause fulminant injury the documented alert is the intervention that prevents the most harm. The drug is already ceased, so management is otherwise supportive with serial monitoring. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)
source_refs: Australian Medicines Handbook
Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Abnormal Liver Function Tests

options.text: Commence oral prednisolone to suppress the immune mediated hepatic inflammation
options.rationale: Corticosteroids have no established role in idiosyncratic drug induced liver injury and the negative autoimmune screen removes the main indication for them. They would be considered if serology and histology supported autoimmune hepatitis. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Abnormal Liver Function Tests)
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Abnormal Liver Function Tests

options.text: Arrange magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography to exclude a retained stone
options.rationale: Ultrasound already shows no biliary dilatation and her pain-free presentation with eosinophilia does not fit obstruction, so further biliary imaging is low yield. It would be justified if the alkaline phosphatase pattern dominated with duct dilatation or pain. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Abnormal Liver Function Tests)
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Abnormal Liver Function Tests

options.text: Prescribe ursodeoxycholic acid to accelerate resolution of the cholestatic component
options.rationale: Evidence for ursodeoxycholic acid in drug induced cholestasis is weak and it does not alter the natural history, so it addresses symptoms at best. Its established indication is primary biliary cholangitis. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)
source_refs: Australian Medicines Handbook

explanation.summary: Drug induced liver injury is a diagnosis of exclusion that depends on establishing a plausible temporal relationship, recognising a drug's known injury signature, and ruling out viral, autoimmune, vascular and obstructive causes. Amoxicillin with clavulanate is among the most frequent causes in Australia, characteristically producing a cholestatic or mixed picture that begins one to six weeks after the course has already finished, which is why patients often no longer connect the two. Hy's law describes the combination of a transaminase rise above three times the upper limit with a bilirubin above twice the upper limit in the absence of biliary obstruction, and identifies patients at risk of a mortality approaching ten per cent. Most cases resolve over weeks to months after withdrawal of the agent, and management is supportive with serial biochemistry and coagulation monitoring. Deliberate rechallenge is contraindicated because the second exposure can produce a far more severe and sometimes fatal reaction.
key_points: Injury may begin weeks after a short course has been completed, obscuring the link
Amoxicillin with clavulanate typically causes a cholestatic or mixed pattern, often with eosinophilia
Hy's law marks a high risk group and requires monitoring of the international normalised ratio
Corticosteroids and ursodeoxycholic acid do not change the course of idiosyncratic injury
Documenting the agent prevents a rechallenge that can be far more severe than the first episode
explanation.pearls: Hy's law is the prognostic trigger: an alanine aminotransferase above three times the upper limit with a bilirubin above twice the upper limit and no obstruction predicts around ten per cent mortality, so track the international normalised ratio rather than the transaminases.

sources.label: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Abnormal Liver Function Tests

subtopic_detail: Fever during the neutrophil nadir after cytotoxic chemotherapy
stem:
You are the medical registrar called to the emergency department to see a 61 year old woman who received her second cycle of chemotherapy for breast cancer nine days ago. She reports feeling shivery since this morning and has a mild sore throat but no cough, dysuria or diarrhoea.

Her tunnelled central line exit site looks clean and non-tender. Chest is clear on auscultation, the abdomen is soft and there are no skin lesions or mucosal ulcers. Intravenous access has been secured and peripheral and line blood cultures have just been drawn. She is alert and speaking in full sentences.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 108/min, BP 112/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 20/min, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 38.4 degrees C
data_table.Investigations: Neutrophils 0.3 x10^9/L (2.0-7.5), white cell count 1.1 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), haemoglobin 104 g/L (115-165), platelets 96 x10^9/L (150-400), creatinine 74 micromol/L (45-90), lactate 1.4 mmol/L (0.5-2.0); chest radiograph shows no focal consolidation

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Give intravenous piperacillin with tazobactam now, without waiting for culture results
options.rationale: Fever with a neutrophil count below 0.5 x10^9/L is a medical emergency in which broad spectrum antipseudomonal beta-lactam therapy should be given within one hour, because clinical signs of infection are blunted and deterioration can be rapid. Cultures have already been taken so nothing further should delay the first dose. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic
eviQ: Febrile Neutropenia

options.text: Give intravenous vancomycin now as single agent empirical cover for line infection
options.rationale: Glycopeptide monotherapy leaves gram negative organisms including Pseudomonas uncovered, and these carry the highest early mortality in this setting. Vancomycin is added to a beta-lactam when there is line site infection, haemodynamic instability or known resistant colonisation. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic

options.text: Give oral amoxicillin with clavulanate and ciprofloxacin and discharge with review
options.rationale: Outpatient oral therapy is confined to carefully selected low risk patients using a validated score, with a short anticipated neutropenia and reliable access to care, and requires an initial period of observation. Her profound neutropenia and tachycardia place her outside that pathway. (Source: eviQ: Febrile Neutropenia)
source_refs: eviQ: Febrile Neutropenia

options.text: Give a granulocyte colony stimulating factor injection and repeat the count in six hours
options.rationale: Colony stimulating factors do not treat established infection and take days to raise the neutrophil count, so relying on one delays the intervention that saves lives. Their role is primary or secondary prophylaxis between cycles. (Source: eviQ: Febrile Neutropenia)
source_refs: eviQ: Febrile Neutropenia

options.text: Give intravenous fluids and paracetamol and repeat the observations in two hours
options.rationale: Antipyresis without antibiotics masks the only reliable sign of infection she has while the underlying process continues, and each hour of delay increases mortality. Supportive measures accompany antibiotics rather than substituting for them. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic

explanation.summary: Febrile neutropenia is defined as a single temperature of 38.5 degrees C or a sustained temperature of 38.0 degrees C for an hour, together with a neutrophil count below 0.5 x10^9/L or below 1.0 x10^9/L and falling. The neutrophil nadir typically occurs seven to 14 days after cytotoxic chemotherapy, and because the inflammatory response is impaired, the usual localising signs of pneumonia, cellulitis or abscess may be absent. Empirical monotherapy with an antipseudomonal beta-lactam is the standard first line, and the interval from presentation to first dose is the quality measure that correlates with survival. Additional gram positive cover is layered on for specific indications rather than given routinely, and antifungal therapy is considered when fever persists beyond four to seven days. Risk scoring identifies a low risk subgroup who may be managed with oral antibiotics, but the default is admission for intravenous therapy.
key_points: The nadir falls seven to 14 days after chemotherapy, so ask the date of the last cycle
Neutropenia blunts localising signs, so a normal chest radiograph does not exclude pneumonia
An antipseudomonal beta-lactam is the empirical backbone; vancomycin is added only for specific indications
Colony stimulating factors are prophylaxis between cycles, not treatment for established fever
Persistent fever beyond four to seven days prompts consideration of invasive fungal infection
explanation.pearls: The door-to-antibiotic interval is the number that matters: the first dose of an antipseudomonal beta-lactam should be given within 60 minutes of presentation, taking blood cultures on the way rather than waiting for them.
